doctitle: UDL Supports — Critical Thinking Online Breakouts
lead: Practical ways to open these Critical Thinking Online Breakouts to every learner, organized by the three principles of the CAST Universal Design for Learning Guidelines (version 3.0). Each breakout already builds in many of these supports; the suggestions below help you extend them.
goal: 🎯 The goal of UDL is learner agency — learners who are purposeful & reflective, resourceful & authentic, and strategic & action-oriented. Design for the edges and the whole class benefits.
howto: 🧑‍🏫 How to use this page: each of the three principles below lists CAST's design options (with their guideline numbers), then a “In these breakouts” box with concrete moves you can make today. Pair it with the ELPS supports page for emergent bilingual learners and the lesson-plan guide for a ready structure.
eng.sub: the “why” of learning — recruit interest, sustain effort, and support self-regulation
a7.list:
• Optimize choice and autonomy (7.1)
  • Optimize relevance, value, and authenticity (7.2)
  • Nurture joy and play (7.3)
  • Address biases, threats, and distractions (7.4)
a8.list:
• Clarify the meaning and purpose of goals (8.1)
  • Optimize challenge and support (8.2)
  • Foster collaboration, interdependence, and collective learning (8.3)
  • Foster belonging and community (8.4)
  • Offer action-oriented feedback (8.5)
a9.list:
• Recognize expectations, beliefs, and motivations (9.1)
  • Develop awareness of self and others (9.2)
  • Promote individual and collective reflection (9.3)
  • Cultivate empathy and restorative practices (9.4)
eng.apply: In these breakouts: the four locks turn content into a playful puzzle to solve, not a test to pass (7.3). Nothing is graded and students can Start over as often as they like, so mistakes cost nothing and effort is safe (8.2, 9.1). Let students pick their own language with the 🌐 menu and choose to work solo or with a partner (7.1). The progress dots and “locks open” count make the goal visible and celebrate each step (8.1, 8.5). Assign pairs or small teams so students reason out loud together (8.3, 8.4), and close with a quick reflection on which clue cracked each lock (9.3).
rep.sub: the “what” of learning — perception, language and symbols, and building knowledge
a1.list:
• Support opportunities to customize the display of information (1.1)
  • Support multiple ways to perceive information (1.2)
  • Represent a diversity of perspectives and identities in authentic ways (1.3)
a2.list:
• Clarify vocabulary, symbols, and language structures (2.1)
  • Support decoding of text, mathematical notation, and symbols (2.2)
  • Cultivate understanding and respect across languages and dialects (2.3)
  • Address biases in the use of language and symbols (2.4)
  • Illustrate through multiple media (2.5)
a3.list:
• Connect prior knowledge to new learning (3.1)
  • Highlight and explore patterns, critical features, big ideas, and relationships (3.2)
  • Cultivate multiple ways of knowing and making meaning (3.3)
  • Maximize transfer and generalization (3.4)
rep.apply: In these breakouts: every activity runs in seven languages from the 🌐 menu, so multilingual learners can read the same idea in their home language and in English (2.3, 1.1). Clue cards chunk information into short, tappable pieces students can reopen any time (1.1, 3.2). Where a suite includes a word bank or glossary, pre-teach it to clarify vocabulary and symbols (2.1, 2.2). The evidence-sort lock asks students to separate strong evidence from a true-but-off-topic fact, making the “big idea vs. detail” distinction explicit (3.2). Activate prior knowledge before starting and name where the idea shows up elsewhere to support transfer (3.1, 3.4).
act.sub: the “how” of learning — interaction, expression and communication, and strategy
a4.list:
• Vary and honor the methods for response, navigation, and movement (4.1)
  • Optimize access to accessible materials and assistive and accessible technologies and tools (4.2)
a5.list:
• Use multiple media for communication (5.1)
  • Use multiple tools for construction, composition, and creativity (5.2)
  • Build fluencies with graduated support for practice and performance (5.3)
  • Address biases related to modes of expression and communication (5.4)
a6.list:
• Set meaningful goals (6.1)
  • Anticipate and plan for challenges (6.2)
  • Organize information and resources (6.3)
  • Enhance capacity for monitoring progress (6.4)
  • Challenge exclusionary practices (6.5)
act.apply: In these breakouts: the four lock types ask for the answer in different ways — ordering a sequence, choosing from options, sorting evidence, and typing a word — so students show what they know through more than one channel (5.1, 4.1). Everything works with mouse, touch, or keyboard and runs in the browser with no login, so it pairs cleanly with a screen reader, zoom, or a district assistive-tech tool (4.2). The word lock accepts spelling variants, lowering the cost of encoding while students build fluency (5.3). Have students narrate their strategy — which clue, which lock, why — to make thinking visible and monitor their own progress (6.3, 6.4).
wins.list:
• Let students choose the language. Show the 🌐 menu before you begin — it is a support, not an accommodation to request.
  • Pair, don’t isolate. Two students per device turns each lock into a reasoning conversation.
  • Normalize “Start over.” Say out loud that retrying is how the game is played.
  • Debrief the decoy. Ask why the off-topic fact was true but did not help — that is the critical-thinking payoff.
  • Connect it forward. End by naming one place this idea shows up outside the screen.
